title: Evidence & measurement
blurb: The traps that wreck city analytics: selection, small numbers, shifting mixes and measures that become targets.

cards.prompt: A hot-spot intervention targets the 10 blocks with the most incidents last quarter, and incidents drop the next quarter. Why isn't that evidence it worked?
cards.answer: Regression to the mean. Blocks picked because they had an extreme period tend to look more typical the next period whether or not anything was done. You need a comparison group selected the same way, or longer pre-intervention trends.
points: Regression to the mean happens without any intervention
Comparison group chosen the same way, or longer pre-trends
cards.source: Standard; see Campbell & Ross (1968) on the Connecticut speeding crackdown

cards.answer: The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor.
cards.why: Close relative of Goodhart's law (popular form, after Strathern): when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
cards.source: Donald T. Campbell, Assessing the Impact of Planned Social Change (1979)

cards.prompt: What is the identifying assumption of difference-in-differences?
cards.answer: Parallel trends: absent the treatment, the treated and comparison groups would have changed by the same amount.
cards.why: Check the pre-period trends, and look for anything else that changed at the same time.

cards.prompt: Why do 'top 10 tracts by rate' lists keep featuring tiny tracts, and what do you do about it?
cards.answer: Small denominators make rates noisy, so by chance small areas fill both the top and the bottom of the ranking. Use funnel plots, empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the overall rate, minimum denominators, or pooled years, and show the uncertainty.
points: Small denominators produce extreme rates in both directions
cards.source: Gelman & Price, All maps of parameter estimates are misleading (1999)

cards.prompt: A council member asks for 'the 10 worst blocks for code violations' from raw counts. What do you ask and adjust before you send a list?
cards.answer: Normalize per parcel or housing unit rather than using raw counts. Raise detection bias: violations reflect where inspectors go and who complains, because enforcement is largely complaint-driven. Small numbers make rankings unstable, so pool time or shrink the rates. Pin down the time window and which violations count (open or closed, severity). Ask what decision the list is for, and present it with uncertainty and context.
points: Ask what decision it informs; show uncertainty

cards.prompt: Average 311 response time improved in every district, yet the citywide average got worse. How?
cards.answer: Simpson's paradox. The mix shifted: more requests now come from districts or request types with long response times, so the weighted average rises even though every subgroup improved. Report stratified figures or standardize the mix.
points: Weighted average can move against every subgroup
